description: Our goal: a tool that picks Earth science variables, shows how they change, and tests whether trends are statistically significant. I cover data, statistics and agents. Looking for: Earth science knowledge, frontend/visualization and web development. Beginners welcome, two days, one working prototype.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a multi-agent AI system that answers plain-language questions about climate trends in Italy using NASA POWER data. Ask "Is it raining more in southern Italy?" and an AI planner chooses which of the 20 regional capitals and which variables to analyse. Python then runs the statistics: a seasonal Mann-Kendall test, a Sen slope with confidence intervals, and a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across zones. A second AI agent explains the results, and a deterministic guardrail checks every claim before the answer is shown. The AI never writes a number: it uses placeholders that code fills in.

This addresses the core of the challenge: telling real trends from noise, and saying so honestly. From 1981 to 2024, temperature rose significantly in all 20 capitals, from +0.22 °C per decade in Palermo to +0.52 °C in Bologna. For rainfall, only Bologna shows a significant change, a decrease. Three other cities look significant on their own, but not after correcting for 20 tests. It matters because climate claims are often confident but untested. This tool makes rigorous trend detection accessible to anyone while keeping the AI honest.
details:
What it does
Users ask questions in natural language (for example "Are the Alps warming faster than Sicily?"). The app returns a verified answer with trend charts, the numbers behind it, the analysis plan and the guardrail report. It covers air temperature at 2 m (T2M) and corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), using monthly data from 1981 to 2024 for the 20 Italian regional capitals.

How it works
The system is a graph workflow built with Google ADK 2 and Gemini on Vertex AI. One rule runs through it: the LLM decides and explains, the code computes.

  1. Planner (Gemini): turns the question into a typed plan (zones and variables). Questions outside the scope go to a dedicated reply. A region maps to its capital, and a town maps to its region's capital, with a note to the user.
  2. Analysis (Python): downloads NASA POWER data and runs a seasonal Mann-Kendall test with the seasonal Sen slope and its 95% confidence interval. Significance is decided on Benjamini-Hochberg q-values across all 20 zones, so a trend is not called significant just because many places were tested.
  3. Explainer (Gemini): writes the answer using placeholders such as [bologna.T2M.slope_per_decade] instead of numbers.
  4. Guardrail (Python): checks that every placeholder exists and that no digits appear outside placeholders. It checks that the stated directions match the tests, that no forbidden wording is used ("stable", causal claims), and that "faster" is only claimed when the confidence intervals do not overlap. If a check fails, the explainer retries with feedback, up to three attempts. After that, a safe answer is generated by code.

What it found (1981-2024, corrected for 20 tests)

  • Temperature increased significantly in all 20 capitals, from +0.22 °C per decade in Palermo to +0.52 °C per decade in Bologna.
  • Precipitation shows a significant trend only in Bologna, a decrease. Bari, L'Aquila and Perugia have p < 0.05 on their own, but none of them survives the correction.

Why it matters
Climate questions are often answered with confident numbers and no statistics behind them. This tool makes rigorous trend detection accessible to non-experts while keeping the AI honest. Every number comes from code, and every sentence is checked against it.

What makes it creative
Most AI assistants for data generate numbers themselves and can quietly invent them. Here the AI is only allowed to plan and to write, and the code holds it to what was actually computed. The guardrail rejects any digit the AI writes, any direction that contradicts the test, and any "faster" claim when the confidence intervals overlap. Users see not just the answer but also the plan, the raw numbers and the guardrail report, so they can audit every step.

Tools: Python, Google ADK 2, Gemini (Vertex AI), Streamlit, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib, pydantic, uv, pytest (116 tests).

Limitations: each capital is one NASA POWER grid cell, not a regional average. The tool detects trends but does not attribute causes.
